A data dictionary plans every item of data a module uses, including variables, constants, objects and interface controls. Each entry must give a name and a data type at minimum; more columns, for instance a description, a field size, a validation rule or a sample value, are added when useful:

| Name | Data type | Description | Validation |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| binWeights | floating point | the day's bin weights in kg (one-dimensional array) | each 50.0 to 450.0 |
| binCount | integer | number of bins picked today | 0 to 40 |
| ratePerKg | floating point | pay per kilogram, constant 0.11 | |
| dayPay | floating point | the day's pay | |
| totalKg | floating point | running total of the day's bin weights in kg | |
| i | integer | loop counter | |

sections.heading: Object descriptions
sections.body:
An object description plans a single object under three headings. **Name** identifies it, **Properties/Attributes** lists the data it holds (data types are optional), and **Methods** lists its behaviours, each with any parameters it takes.

| Name | Bin |
|:--|:--|
| Properties/Attributes | binID (string), pickerID (string), block (character), weightKg (floating point), isSecondGrade (Boolean) |
| Methods | recordWeight(kg), calculatePay(ratePerKg), markSecondGrade() |

Methods are actions, so `calculatePay` never belongs under Properties/Attributes. A block is one letter from A to H, so it is a character, not a string. Any attribute you add follows the casing already used, here camel casing.

sections.heading: IPO charts and pseudocode
sections.body:
An IPO chart summarises one task in Input, Processes and Output columns, and a module with several tasks gets one chart for each. A process that happens only sometimes must say when.

| Input | Processes | Output |
|:--|:--|:--|
| binWeights, binCount | Add up the bin weights. Multiply the total by ratePerKg to get the day's pay. | dayPay (displayed) |

Pseudocode then sets out the exact steps: `BEGIN` and `END`, keywords in capitals, and the statements inside each control structure indented. The array is indexed from 0:

```pseudo
BEGIN
    totalKg ← 0
    FOR i ← 0 TO binCount - 1
        totalKg ← totalKg + binWeights[i]
    ENDFOR
    dayPay ← totalKg * ratePerKg
    DISPLAY dayPay
END
```

sections.heading: Keeping the tools consistent
sections.body:
The five tools describe one solution, so they must agree with each other:

- each data item has one name and one data type in every tool, so the pseudocode above uses `binWeights` and `dayPay` exactly as the data dictionary spells them
- every input and output in an IPO chart has a data dictionary entry
- each input control on a mock-up maps to data of a fitting type: a *Second grade* check box has only two states, so the data behind it is a Boolean
- a limit noted on a mock-up matches the validation rule in the data dictionary and the check in the pseudocode

A mismatch caught in design costs an edit. The same mismatch caught in code costs a rewrite.

worked.prompt:
The quote module for Corella Point Freight, a Geelong carrier, is designed with this IPO chart:

| Input | Processes | Output |
|:--|:--|:--|
| weightKg, isExpress | Multiply weightKg by 0.85 and add 12.00 to get charge. If isExpress is true, add 18.00 to charge. | charge (displayed) |

Write pseudocode for the module that follows the IPO chart.

points.text: Starts with BEGIN, ends with END, and inputs weightKg and isExpress
Calculates the base charge, e.g. charge ← weightKg * 0.85 + 12.00
Uses selection to add 18.00 only when isExpress is true (IF ... THEN ... ENDIF)
Displays charge after the selection, so the express surcharge is included

worked.model:
```pseudo
BEGIN
    INPUT weightKg
    INPUT isExpress
    charge ← weightKg * 0.85 + 12.00
    IF isExpress THEN
        charge ← charge + 18.00
    ENDIF
    DISPLAY charge
END
```

The surcharge sits inside the IF because the IPO chart applies it only to express consignments, and `charge` is displayed after the IF so the output includes it whenever it applies.

traps: Half of the 2025 cohort scored zero when they had to label two sections of an object description. Use VCAA's own headings: Name, Properties/Attributes and Methods.

When students added attributes to the same object description, names that broke its camel casing earned nothing, and so did data types written as Bool or Float. Write Boolean and floating point in full.

Choosing between four IPO charts in 2025, 80% picked the one whose process stated the condition: the tax-free threshold came off the income only if the user claimed it. The most common wrong pick subtracted the threshold in every case.

intro: User experience (UX) is about how people perceive a digital system and respond as they use it. The study design names four characteristics: affordance, interoperability, usability, and security, which covers authentication and data protection. UX questions were among the worst answered in 2025, and in the sketch comparison, marks went only to answers that used these four names and pointed to the design feature that showed one.

sections.heading: Affordance
sections.body:
Affordance is the degree to which the look of an element tells users what it is for and how to work it. A shaded button with depth invites a press, a box with a blinking cursor invites typing, a down arrow on a field means *choose from a list*, and familiar icons, such as an envelope for messages, need no instructions.

In Corella Point Freight's delivery app, *Delivered* appears as plain text at the bottom of the screen. Drivers don't realise it can be tapped, so some deliveries are never confirmed. Redrawing it as a large green button labelled *Confirm delivery* fixes an affordance problem.

sections.heading: Interoperability
sections.body: Interoperability is a solution's ability to exchange data with other systems and work alongside them. Corella Point's app must pass each confirmed delivery to the firm's accounting program, which already imports CSV files. Designing for interoperability means choosing formats and fields the other system can read, so nobody has to retype data. It isn't portability, which is running on different platforms such as Android and iOS.

sections.heading: Security: authentication and data protection
sections.body:
Authentication confirms that users are who they claim to be, through a sign-in, a PIN or a fingerprint, and a log out control lets them end the session. Data protection keeps information from people who shouldn't see it: nothing personal on screen before sign-in, each role seeing only what it needs, and stored data encrypted.

Users notice these features, and they shape trust. A screen headed *Signed in as R. Okafor* that lists only that driver's deliveries shows the driver has been authenticated, and that customers' addresses aren't open to every user. Each security step also adds effort, so good design keeps the steps few, such as a fingerprint instead of a long password on a phone the firm issued.

sections.heading: Usability
sections.body: Usability is how easily the intended users can learn a solution and use it to complete their tasks, including users with a disability. Corella Point's drivers record dozens of deliveries a shift, often one-handed beside the truck. Filling in the date and time automatically, choosing the consignment from today's list instead of typing its number, and confirming each save with a clear message all cut the steps and the errors.

sections.heading: Comparing two designs
sections.body:
Questions often show two sketches or a mock-up and ask which characteristic a design shows better, or needs most. A full answer does three things:

1. Names one of the four characteristics.
2. Points to the feature that shows it, such as a log out button for security or a drop-down list for usability.
3. Says what the other design lacks, such as private details on show before anyone signs in.

Keep UX characteristics apart from design principles. Contrast, alignment and navigation are design principles, so they earn nothing when a UX characteristic is asked for. Usability is the one name that appears on both lists.

worked.prompt:
Yarrowee Mobile Vets in Ballarat is designing a tablet app that its vets use on farm visits. The app shows each farm's address and contact details and the treatment history of its animals. Two features in the design are:

1. After each visit, the treatments given are sent to the practice's billing program in a file format that the billing program already imports.
2. The app locks after two minutes without use, and the vet's PIN or fingerprint is needed to unlock it.

For each feature, identify the characteristic of user experience it most improves, and explain how it improves the experience of the vets or their clients.

points.text: Feature 1: interoperability
Explains: treatments reach the billing program without office staff retyping them, so bills are ready sooner and match what the vet recorded, and vets don't enter anything twice
Feature 2: security (authentication)
Explains: if a tablet is left in a ute or a shed, no one else can see farms' contact details or animal records, while a fingerprint lets the vet unlock it with little effort

worked.model:
The first feature improves interoperability. The app exchanges data with another system, the billing program, in a format that program already reads. Treatments flow straight into billing without office staff retyping them, so clients' bills are ready sooner and match what the vet actually recorded, with no copying errors.

The second feature improves security, through authentication. A vet often puts the tablet down in a ute or a shed during a visit. Because it locks after two minutes and only the vet's PIN or fingerprint opens it, nobody who picks it up can read the farms' contact details or their animals' records. The fingerprint option keeps unlocking quick, so the protection costs the vet very little effort.

traps: Asked which UX characteristic a mock-up most needed to improve, 55% correctly chose affordance. A quarter chose contrast, which is a design principle and not one of the four UX characteristics.

Comparing two sketches in 2025, 59% of students scored zero and 2% scored full marks. Answers that didn't name a UX characteristic from the study design earned nothing. Credited answers pointed to the feature that showed the characteristic, such as a logout button and a heading showing the user's role for security, icons people already know for affordance, or a drop-down list in place of typing for usability, and said what the other sketch lacked.
Few students noticed that one sketch seemed to show private tenant and property details to anyone, with no login at all. Look for a weakness like that when you compare two designs for security.

intro: Design principles are accepted qualities that shape how an interface looks and works. This point lists seven: alignment, balance, contrast, space, text formatting, usability and navigation. You need to be able to apply one to a screen, justify a choice with one, or spot the principle a mock-up fails, always for the users in the scenario.

sections.heading: Alignment, balance and space
sections.body:
These three decide where things sit.

- **Alignment** lines elements up along shared edges or centres. On Corella Point Freight's consignment form, every label starts at the same left edge and every text box at a second one, so the eye runs straight down the fields.
- **Balance** spreads visual weight across the screen. It can be symmetrical, or asymmetrical, such as a large map on the left offset by a group of smaller controls on the right.
- **Space** is the empty area around and between elements. Margins stop a screen feeling cramped, and a wider gap between the sender's details and the receiver's details than between fields within each group shows which fields belong together.

sections.heading: Contrast and text formatting
sections.body:
**Contrast** makes elements clearly different in colour, size, weight or shape, so the important ones stand out and text is readable against its background. Dark text on a light background still works in a sunny depot yard; pale grey on white doesn't. Contrast shouldn't rely on colour alone, because some users can't tell red from green.

**Text formatting** covers the font, its size and colour, and enhancements such as bold. A large bold heading shows what a screen is for, one or two fonts keep it calm, and bold is saved for what matters, such as *Fragile*. Mock-up annotations record these choices.

sections.heading: Usability and navigation
sections.body: These two are about how the interface works as much as how it looks. As a design principle, **usability** means ease of use and accessibility: controls big enough to tap wearing gloves, text that can be enlarged, and as few steps as possible to finish a task. **Navigation** is how users move between screens and keep track of where they are: menus, tabs, and Back and Next buttons with the same label and position on every screen, plus a marker such as *Step 2 of 4*.

sections.heading: Principles are not UX characteristics
sections.body: The study design keeps two separate lists. Design principles describe how an interface is laid out and behaves. The UX characteristics (affordance, interoperability, security and usability) describe how people experience the whole solution. Contrast is a principle, so it is the wrong answer when a question asks for a UX characteristic. Usability is the only term on both lists.

sections.heading: Justifying a design choice
sections.body:
A justification names the principle, points to the feature on the screen, and says what it does for these particular users. For the depot's forklift drivers, who glance at a wall tablet between loads:

*Contrast: the Next load panel is white text on dark blue, unlike the grey panels around it, so a driver can find the next job with one look across the yard.*

Naming a principle without the feature and the users' need doesn't justify anything.

worked.prompt:
Kestrel Downs Orchards in Shepparton has a tablet on the packing-shed wall where pickers check their tally for the week. The draft screen shows each day's bins in a table of small, pale grey text, and the week's total is in the same size and style as the daily rows. To change week, pickers tap one of 52 small numbered buttons squeezed into a strip along the bottom of the screen. Pickers often wear gloves, and many read English as an additional language.

Recommend **two** changes to the screen. For each change, name the design principle it applies and justify it with reference to the pickers.

points.text: First change with its principle, e.g. text formatting: dark, larger text for the daily rows and the week's total in large bold type with a clear label (contrast is also accepted)
Justifies it for the pickers, e.g. they find the figure they came for at a glance, without reading every row, which helps those with less English
Second change with its principle, e.g. usability: replace the 52 small buttons with large Previous week and Next week buttons (navigation is also accepted)
Justifies it for the pickers, e.g. large buttons can be tapped accurately with gloves on, so pickers stop landing on the wrong week

worked.model:
First, apply text formatting. The daily rows should be in dark text at a larger size, and the week's total should be in large bold type with a clear label such as *Week total*, set apart from the rows. Pickers come to the screen to see that total, so making it stand out lets them find it at a glance without working through the table, which matters for pickers who read English as an additional language.

Second, apply usability. The strip of 52 small buttons should be replaced with two large buttons, *Previous week* and *Next week*, with the current week's dates shown between them. Pickers wearing gloves can't tap small, crowded buttons accurately, so they often land on the wrong week. Two large buttons are easy to hit with a gloved finger, and the dates show which week is on screen.

traps: On the 2025 paper, a quarter of students answered *contrast* when asked which UX characteristic a mock-up most needed to improve. Contrast is a design principle; the answer was affordance, a UX characteristic.
